title: Outbreak Mapping

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Outbreak mapping is the work of turning case reports, laboratory results and syndromic signals into a picture of where a disease is, how fast it is moving and who is at risk. In epidemiology and population health it covers routine surveillance, cluster detection, epidemic forecasting and the situational reports that health agencies publish during an emergency. The field sits between classical field epidemiology and data science, and it draws on case definitions, denominators and reporting delays as much as on any model.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The inputs are notifiable disease reports, electronic health records, laboratory confirmations, wastewater sampling, mobility data and open feeds such as those published by national public health agencies and the World Health Organization. These arrive at different speeds and different geographies, so pipelines must reconcile case counts with specimen dates, population estimates and reporting lags before anything is mapped. Outputs are typically dashboards, choropleth maps, nowcasts and short forecasts, often delivered through the same platforms that feed the site's catalogue of medical AI models.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start with case definitions and data cleaning, then apply statistical detection methods such as space time scan statistics for clusters and time series models for trends. Forecasts usually combine mechanistic epidemic models with statistical or machine learning components, and every estimate carries an interval because counts are incomplete and revised. Validation is done by backtesting against past outbreaks and by comparing model output with field investigation, since a map is only as good as the case ascertainment behind it.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Outbreak data is sensitive because it can identify individuals, stigmatise places and trigger economic consequences, so access is usually tiered and small area counts are suppressed or aggregated. Provenance matters: agencies need to know which source produced a number, when it was last updated and whether it was revised. Legal and ethical duties around privacy, mandatory reporting and emergency powers sit alongside the technical work, and the site's compliance and regulation pages track how these obligations are being written into practice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward faster integration of genomic, wastewater and clinical signals, with uncertainty reported rather than hidden. Expect more emphasis on open standards for data exchange, on reproducible pipelines that can be audited after an event, and on models that are evaluated in real outbreaks rather than only on historical data. The harder problems are institutional: timeliness of reporting, equity in who gets counted, and clear communication of what a map does and does not show.
